e2d1a6bf7221: The Big Book makes honesty a condition of recovery. Those who don't recover are usually people "constitutionally incapable of being honest with themselves" (<0>p. 58</0>), and the program is "a manner of living which demands rigorous honesty" (<1>p. 58</1>). Of people with grave emotional and mental disorders, "many of them do recover if they have the capacity to be honest." (<2>p. 58</2>)
06b232d153f0: Honesty with oneself comes first: diagnosing yourself honestly (<0>pp. 32</0>, 44), taking stock without fooling yourself (<1>p. 64</1>), and searching out "selfish, dishonest, self-seeking and frightened" conduct in the inventory (<2>p. 67</2>).
2292b176923f: It doesn't stop at self-knowledge. The Fifth Step chapter says "We must be entirely honest with somebody if we expect to live long or happily in this world." (<0>pp. 73–74</0>), and dishonesty is one of the four things the Step Ten passage says to keep watching for (<1>p. 84</1>).
c1b2821f3b35: The book does not make honesty a licence to hurt people. In the Fifth Step, the amends and family life it repeatedly limits what we disclose when it would harm someone else (<0>pp. 74</0>, 80–82, 125). It never uses the phrase "absolute honesty."
4db8edeb1d67: Chapter 5 begins with honesty. People who don't recover "cannot or will not completely give themselves to this simple program," usually because they are "constitutionally incapable of being honest with themselves" (<0>p. 58</0>). The book adds: "They are not at fault; they seem to have been born that way." (<1>p. 58</1>), and that they can't grasp "a manner of living which demands rigorous honesty" (<2>p. 58</2>). "Their chances are less than average." (<3>p. 58</3>) Then the hopeful line about people with grave emotional and mental disorders: "many of them do recover if they have the capacity to be honest." (<4>p. 58</4>). See: <5>What does "Rarely have we seen a person fail" really say, and who does it say may not recover?</5>
6a7fac84de6d: <0>About whether you are alcoholic.</0> Try some controlled drinking: "It will not take long for you to decide, if you are honest with yourself about it." (<1>p. 32</1>). Chapter 4 opens: "If, when you honestly want to, you find you cannot quit entirely," you are probably alcoholic (<2>p. 44</2>). Chapter 3 says many real alcoholics will try "By every form of self-deception and experimentation" to prove they're exceptions (<3>p. 31</3>).
af18c76048af: <0>About why you drank.</0> Asked why he started the last bender, the alcoholic offers alibis; "Once in a while he may tell the truth." and the truth is usually that he has no more idea why than you do (<1>p. 23</1>).
e1862791bd60: <0>In the inventory.</0> The business owner taking stock "cannot fool himself about values." (<1>p. 64</1>), and so "We took stock honestly." (<2>p. 64</2>). "Nothing counted but thoroughness and honesty." (<3>p. 65</3>). Each resentment is turned around to ask "Where had we been selfish, dishonest, self-seeking and frightened?" (<4>p. 67</4>), and "We admitted our wrongs honestly" (<5>p. 67</5>). The sex inventory asks the same: "Where had we been selfish, dishonest, or inconsiderate?" (<6>p. 69</6>). The book's picture of the real alcoholic is that about liquor "he is incredibly dishonest and selfish." (<7>p. 21</7>)
d5d9891f60a7: <0>About God.</0> The agnostic chapter asks the reader to be honest about spiritual terms too: don't let prejudice keep you "from honestly asking yourself what they mean to you." (<1>p. 47</1>), and "He has come to all who have honestly sought Him." (<2>p. 57</2>).
2c56ee3319d7: Chapter 6 argues that self-honesty alone usually isn't enough. Newcomers who kept certain facts to themselves almost always got drunk (<0>pp. 72–73</0>): "they had not learned enough of humility, fearlessness and honesty, in the sense we find it necessary, until they told someone else all their life story." (<1>p. 73</1>). Of their doctors the writers admit "We have seldom told them the whole truth" (<2>p. 73</2>), and "Unwilling to be honest with these sympathetic men, we were honest with no one else." (<3>p. 73</3>). The conclusion: "We must be entirely honest with somebody if we expect to live long or happily in this world." (<4>pp. 73–74</4>). See: <5>Who do I tell my Fifth Step to?</5>
b4ec655a86b6: Steps Eight and Nine carry honesty out into the world. Amends are made with a manner that is "calm, frank, and open" (<0>p. 78</0>). Creditors are told what we're trying to do, and "we make no bones about our drinking" (<1>p. 78</1>). Some people can't be seen, so "we send them an honest letter." (<2>p. 83</2>). The book tells of a man who had slandered a business rival and, after consulting his wife and partner, stood up in church and set the record straight (<3>p. 80</3>).
d00c39362ea4: Step Ten: "Continue to watch for selfishness, dishonesty, resentment, and fear." (<0>p. 84</0>), asking God at once to remove them. Step Eleven's nightly review asks "Were we resentful, selfish, dishonest or afraid?" (<1>p. 86</1>), and the morning asks that our thinking "be divorced from self-pity, dishonest or self-seeking motives." (<2>p. 86</2>). In Chapter 10 an employer is told our solution "demands rigorous honesty" (<3>p. 145</3>), and that a man still trying to recover, if he does drink, will tell the employer "even if it means the loss of his job. For he knows he must be honest if he would live at all." (<4>p. 146</4>).
768dec4522a9: The book that demands rigorous honesty also says, more than once, not to buy our own relief at someone else's cost:
6ecd27ca9e0d: In the Fifth Step: "we cannot disclose anything to our wives or our parents which will hurt them and make them unhappy. We have no right to save our own skin at another person's expense." (<0>p. 74</0>). Those parts go to "someone who will understand, yet be unaffected" (<1>p. 74</1>). "The rule is we must be hard on ourself, but always considerate of others." (<2>p. 74</2>)
0b34be9c328a: In amends: before drastic action that might implicate others, "we secure their consent." (<0>p. 80</0>). The step reads "except when to do so would injure them or others" (<1>p. 59</1>).
9efc28b3e61c: About an affair: a man should admit his fault, but "we have no right to involve another person" (<0>p. 81</0>), and it's better "that one does not needlessly name a person" (<1>p. 82</1>). The book says "Perhaps there are some cases where the utmost frankness is demanded." and "No outsider can appraise such an intimate situation." (<2>p. 82</2>)
3ce193931578: In the family: unless some good and useful purpose is served, "past occurrences should not be discussed." (<0>p. 125</0>). And "we do not relate intimate experiences of another person unless we are sure he would approve." (<1>p. 125</1>)
0a9bacd137d1: So the honesty the book asks for is complete toward oneself, toward God and toward at least one other person, and careful toward everyone the truth could hurt. See: <0>How does the Big Book say to make amends?</0> and <1>Is "we're only as sick as our secrets" in the Big Book?</1>
5ff55a8d3686: Appendix II, written after the first printing (<0>p. 567</0>) and in the book's appendices since the second edition of 1955 (<1>p. xi</1>), says "any alcoholic capable of honestly facing his problems in the light of our experience can recover" provided he doesn't close his mind to all spiritual concepts (<2>p. 568</2>), and names three essentials: "Willingness, honesty and open mindedness are the essentials of recovery." (<3>p. 568</3>). The 1939 Foreword gave membership's only requirement as "an honest desire to stop drinking." (<4>p. xiv</4>); the short form of the Third Tradition now reads "The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking." (<5>p. 562</5>), without the word. Bill W.'s 1946 Grapevine piece on membership quotes the 1939 wording and tells how the groups' many membership rules, had they all been enforced, would have kept out nearly every early member (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?," 1946). See: <6>What is the only requirement for membership?</6>

65f72d8d938f: Falling short doesn't by itself mean a drunk ("It depends on us and on our motives," <0>p. 70</0>): if we are sorry and want to do better, "we believe we will be forgiven" (<1>p. 70</1>); if we aren't sorry and keep harming others, "we are quite sure to drink" (<2>p. 70</2>). When sex is very troublesome, "we throw ourselves the harder into helping others" (<3>p. 70</3>).
f3ecfa3d6ec3: It also comes up in the resentment inventory (<0>pp. 64–65</0>), in amends for an affair (<1>pp. 80–82</1>), and in a frank note on impotence after drinking stops (<2>p. 134</2>).
4bdbdfad0c14: The passage follows the fear inventory and opens: "Now about sex. Many of us needed an overhauling there." (<0>p. 68</0>) Then, in order:
53a14047679f: <0>1. Stay sensible and out of the argument.</0> "But above all, we tried to be sensible on this question." (<1>p. 68</1>) The book describes opinion running to "absurd extremes" (<2>p. 68</2>): one side calls sex "a lust of our lower nature" (<3>p. 68</3>), the other cries "for sex and more sex" (<4>p. 69</4>). "One school would allow man no flavor for his fare and the other would have us all on a straight pepper diet." (<5>p. 69</5>) Its answer: "We want to stay out of this controversy." (<6>p. 69</6>) "We all have sex problems. We'd hardly be human if we didn't." (<7>p. 69</7>)
582f0e4fadf8: <0>2. Look at our own conduct.</0> The questions are about how we treated people, not about rules (<1>p. 69</1>):
4fb16d0f7fe3: "Where had we been selfish, dishonest, or inconsiderate?" (<0>p. 69</0>)
58bc60fe37b3: "Did we unjustifiably arouse jealousy, suspicion or bitterness?" (<0>p. 69</0>)
43c28082e40d: Where were we at fault, and what should we have done instead? (<0>p. 69</0>)
7c17218d3392: "We got this all down on paper and looked at it." (<0>p. 69</0>)
89f54f1ed08f: <0>3. Shape an ideal.</0> "In this way we tried to shape a sane and sound ideal for our future sex life." (<1>p. 69</1>) Each relation was put to one test: "was it selfish or not?" (<1>p. 69</1>) We must be willing to make amends where we've done harm, "provided that we do not bring about still more harm in so doing" (<2>p. 69</2>). "In other words, we treat sex as we would any other problem." (<3>p. 69</3>) In meditation we ask God what to do about each specific matter: "The right answer will come, if we want it." (<4>p. 69</4>)

f73ff5b2710b: What does the Big Book say about tolerance?
79e69d081104: Tolerance in the Big Book is almost always about people: those who wronged us, our families, each other, drinkers, and people whose opinions or religion differ from ours. It's best known from "Love and tolerance of others is our code." (<0>p. 84</0>), the close of the Step Ten paragraph.
acc903cee785: The book ties it to seeing others as sick. In the resentment inventory, members asked God to help them show people who hurt them "the same tolerance, pity, and patience that we would cheerfully grant a sick friend." (<0>p. 67</0>), and finishing the inventory, "We have begun to learn tolerance, patience and good will toward all men, even our enemies" (<1>p. 70</1>).
b395aa6fe174: The book counts intolerance as a real danger. It admits "We talked of intolerance, while we were intolerant ourselves." (<0>p. 50</0>), warns that a spirit of intolerance toward drinking "might repel alcoholics whose lives could have been saved" (<1>p. 103</1>), and tells a wife that "The slightest sign of fear or intolerance may lessen your husband's chance of recovery." (<2>p. 120</2>).
e737f872d304: Where the writers seek it for themselves, they ask God for it (<0>pp. 67</0>, 83); at the end of the inventory they say they "have begun to learn" it (<1>p. 70</1>). And on the same page as the family amends, the book says being considerate and humble doesn't mean crawling: "As God's people we stand on our feet; we don't crawl before anyone." (<2>p. 83</2>).
8bdce6b1e193: The book uses "tolerance," "tolerant," "intolerance" or "intolerant" on <0>pp. 19</0>, 50, 67, 70, 83, 84, 103, 118, 120, 122, 125, 127, 135, 138 and 160 of the main text, and on <1>p. 568</1> in Appendix II. Read in order:
be2c2bad36a6: <0>Other people's views (<1>p. 19</1>).</0> Introducing the book, the writers know medical, psychiatric and religious matters are controversial and hope to avoid contention: "Most of us sense that real tolerance of other people's shortcomings and viewpoints and a respect for their opinions are attitudes which make us more useful to others." (<2>pp. 19–20</2>)
7eac4cfc0ff6: <0>Religious people (<1>p. 50</1>).</0> Chapter 4 confesses how the agnostics among them used to judge believers by their defects: "We talked of intolerance, while we were intolerant ourselves." (<2>p. 50</2>) They "missed the reality and the beauty of the forest because we were diverted by the ugliness of some of its trees." (<3>p. 50</3>)
043a87ce5856: <0>People who wronged us (<1>pp. 67</1>, 70).</0> In the resentment inventory, the writers realized the people who hurt them "were perhaps spiritually sick" (<2>p. 66</2>) and asked God to help them show those people tolerance, pity and patience (<3>p. 67</3>). "We cannot be helpful to all people, but at least God will show us how to take a kindly and tolerant view of each and every one." (<4>p. 67</4>). At the end of the inventory: tolerance, patience and good will "even our enemies, for we look on them as sick people." (<5>p. 70</5>). See: <6>Does the Big Book really say to pray for people you resent ("This is a sick man")?</6>
a86f9b8b8e3a: <0>The family, in the amends (<1>p. 83</1>).</0> The recovering man cleans house with the family, "asking each morning in meditation that our Creator show us the way of patience, tolerance, kindliness and love." (<2>p. 83</2>)
263359a2e8bf: <0>The code (<1>p. 84</1>).</0> After the Step Ten instructions (watch for selfishness, dishonesty, resentment and fear, ask God to remove them, talk them over, make amends, turn to someone we can help): "Love and tolerance of others is our code." (<2>p. 84</2>). The book's next sentence is "And we have ceased fighting anything or anyone—even alcohol." (<3>p. 84</3>). See: <4>Where is "love and tolerance of others is our code"?</4>
dc233dacd9a5: <0>Drinking and drinkers (<1>p. 103</1>).</0> At the end of Chapter 7: "We are careful never to show intolerance or hatred of drinking as an institution." (<2>p. 103</2>). Every newcomer looks for this and "is immensely relieved when he finds we are not witchburners." (<3>p. 103</3>). The book doesn't argue about whether members keep liquor at home; "each family, in the light of their own circumstances, ought to decide for themselves." (<4>pp. 102–103</4>)
3835c1d699ab: <0>A wife toward her husband (<1>pp. 118</1>, 120).</0> "Patience, tolerance, understanding and love are the watchwords." (<2>p. 118</2>), and "Live and let live is the rule." (<3>p. 118</3>). Later: "The slightest sign of fear or intolerance may lessen your husband's chance of recovery." (<4>p. 120</4>), because he may take her dislike of his friends as an excuse to drink (<5>p. 120</5>).
6b509ffd649e: <0>The whole family (<1>pp. 122</1>, 127).</0> Chapter 9 opens: "All members of the family should meet upon the common ground of tolerance, understanding and love." (<2>p. 122</2>), and says at once that this "involves a process of deflation" (<3>p. 122</3>) because each one wants his wishes respected. The father's crankiness and depression "will disappear when there is tolerance, love, and spiritual understanding." (<4>p. 127</4>)

d7be32d50f13: Bill W. was William Griffith Wilson (1895–1971), one of A.A.'s two co-founders (P-53, 2017); the Big Book's Foreword to the Second Edition calls him "a New York stockbroker" (p. xv). His own story, written in 1939, is Chapter 1 of the Big Book, "Bill's Story" (pp. 1–16).
6114fa49b21a: His drinking began in the army in the First World War, ruined a Wall Street career, and ended in Towns Hospital in December 1934, after a sober old friend (Ebby) had come to his kitchen with "a simple religious idea and a practical program of action" (<0>p. 9</0>). He writes, "I have not had a drink since." (<1>p. 13</1>).
bdbf695d29c3: Working with other alcoholics was, from the start, how he stayed sober: "when all other measures failed, work with another alcoholic would save the day." (<0>p. 15</0>). Looking for one in Akron in May 1935 led him to Dr. Bob (P-53, 2017), and the Big Book dates the first group's spark to Akron in June 1935 (p. xv).
4e150b1c75d2: He drafted the Big Book's chapters (1939) (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957) and codified the Traditions (1946), helped set up the trustees (1938) and the General Service Conference (1951), and stepped down from active leadership in 1955 (P-53, 2017), the year he turned A.A.'s affairs over to the Conference at St. Louis (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957). He died January 24, 1971 (p. 16).
8a2fe8db82f2: The Big Book never gives his full name. The chapter tells the arc in order:
264d90a951b4: <0>The war and the first drinks.</0> A young officer from Plattsburg in a New England town, flattered by the first citizens, "in the midst of the excitement I discovered liquor." (<1>p. 1</1>). Sailing for France: "I was very lonely and again turned to alcohol." (<2>p. 1</2>). An inscription on a tombstone at Winchester Cathedral was an "Ominous warning—which I failed to heed." (<3>p. 1</3>).
23748bd28ff8: <0>Wall Street.</0> Home at twenty-two, he took a night law course, worked as an investigator for a surety company, and became interested in the market (<1>p. 2</1>). He and his wife saved $1,000, put it into securities, and spent a year on a motorcycle with a sidecar touring factories for Wall Street; the reports got him a position and an expense account (<2>pp. 2–3</2>). "For the next few years fortune threw money and applause my way." (<3>p. 3</3>). His drinking went on all day and almost every night (<4>p. 3</4>).
67d443395858: <0>The crash and after.</0> October 1929 wiped him out; a friend in Montreal took him on, then had to let him go (<1>p. 4</1>). The couple went to live with his wife's parents; he had "no real employment for five years" (<2>p. 4</2>), while his wife worked in a department store (<3>p. 4</3>). "Liquor ceased to be a luxury; it became a necessity." (<4>p. 5</4>). Resolves and promises failed, and he began to wonder whether he was crazy (<5>pp. 5–6</5>).
232ce701e289: <0>The hospital.</0> Through his brother-in-law, a physician, and his mother, he was placed in a hospital for alcoholics, where "a kind doctor" explained that he had been seriously ill in body and mind (<1>p. 7</1>). Self-knowledge wasn't the answer; he drank again, went back, and his wife was told he would die in delirium tremens or develop a wet brain within a year (<2>p. 7</2>). "Alcohol was my master." (<3>p. 8</3>). He was off again on Armistice Day 1934 (<4>p. 8</4>).
ae55ccfa1744: <0>The old school friend.</0> In late November 1934 an old friend phoned, came over sober, refused a drink and said, "I've got religion." (<1>p. 9</1>). The friend had been shown "a simple religious idea and a practical program of action" (<2>p. 9</2>), and had come to pass it on. Bill's objection to religion was the idea of a God personal to him (p. 10); the friend's answer, "Why don't you choose your own conception of God?" (p. 12), is the turning point of the chapter. See: <3>Who was the old school friend in "Bill's Story" (Ebby)?</3>
8c3ecfac85a4: <0>The last hospital stay.</0> "At the hospital I was separated from alcohol for the last time." (<1>p. 13</1>). There he offered himself to God as he then understood Him, faced his wrongs, and made a list of people he had hurt or resented (<2>p. 13</2>). His friend set out what he was to do: test his thinking, sit quietly when in doubt, pray only for usefulness to others (<3>p. 13</3>). The effect was "electric" (<4>p. 14</4>); he asked the doctor if he was still sane (<5>p. 14</5>). See: <6>What happened to Bill W. at Towns Hospital?</6>
df423b419d09: <0>Working with others.</0> In the hospital the thought came that thousands of hopeless alcoholics "might be glad to have what had been so freely given me" (<1>p. 14</1>). "Faith without works was dead, he said. And how appallingly true for the alcoholic!" (<2>p. 14</2>). He and his wife threw themselves into helping other alcoholics; business associates stayed skeptical for a year and a half (<3>p. 15</3>), and when self-pity and resentment nearly drove him back to drink, "work with another alcoholic would save the day." (<4>p. 15</4>). The chapter ends on a fellowship with "a vast amount of fun about it all" (<5>p. 16</5>) and "deadly earnestness" underneath (<6>p. 16</6>).

177ce80f6bdb: What the 1939 program text asks of a newcomer to begin with is a state of mind, willingness: "Do I now believe, or am I even willing to believe, that there is a Power greater than myself?" (<0>p. 47</0>), and of a doubter, to lay aside prejudice (<1>p. 46</1>). "If he is to find God, the desire must come from within." (<2>p. 95</2>).
5b5aa87cee93: The text does let action come before full belief: starting from a limited conception of God, members later found themselves "accepting many things which then seemed entirely out of reach" (<0>p. 47</0>). The 1939 meeting in Chapter 11 is a place where many a newcomer found his answer (<1>p. 160</1>). One fourth-edition story comes close to the saying: "after some weeks of just showing up, I began to believe that this program could work for me" (<2>p. 474</2>).
6b9dce41cc3e: All our sources were searched for "bring the body," "bring your body," "mind will follow," "will follow," "body and the mind," "the body," "body will," "the mind will," "show up," "showing up," "keep coming back" and "hang around," with page breaks joined. The saying isn't there in any form. The nearest hits are in fourth-edition stories: "after some weeks of just showing up" ("Twice Gifted," <0>p. 474</0>), "suiting up, and showing up for life every day" ("Crossing the River of Denial," <1>p. 337</1>), and, in "Because I'm an Alcoholic," members who "said keep coming back" (<2>p. 344</2>), after which the writer sat silent in the back of meetings for weeks (<3>p. 344</3>).

d457616bde0d: Chapter 4, "We Agnostics," is written to the reader who can't believe. It asks for a state of mind, and very little of it:
16bdf7d9c3fd: "We found that as soon as we were able to lay aside prejudice and express even a willingness to believe in a Power greater than ourselves, we commenced to get results" (<0>p. 46</0>).
a9c108294c19: "We needed to ask ourselves but one short question." (<0>p. 47</0>). "As soon as a man can say that he does believe, or is willing to believe, we emphatically assure him that he is on his way." (<1>p. 47</1>).
5d20bd9adc56: Obstinacy, sensitiveness and unreasoning prejudice: "This sort of thinking had to be abandoned." (<0>p. 48</0>). "Faced with alcoholic destruction, we soon became as open minded on spiritual matters as we had tried to be on other questions." (<1>p. 48</1>).
49df8bc08144: Bill says the same of his own start: "It was only a matter of being willing to believe in a Power greater than myself. Nothing more was required of me to make my beginning." (<0>p. 12</0>). Appendix II, added in 1955, sums it up: "Willingness, honesty and open mindedness are the essentials of recovery." (<1>p. 568</1>).
315a741be50e: Chapter 5's starting line is also about the inside: "If you have decided you want what we have and are willing to go to any length to get it—then you are ready to take certain steps." (<0>p. 58</0>). And Chapter 7 warns the helper not to push: a newcomer "should not be pushed or prodded by you, his wife, or his friends. If he is to find God, the desire must come from within." (<1>p. 95</1>).

e8e1286fbc52: The saying's real point, that doing comes before understanding, does have support in the 1939 text, as long as willingness is there first:
3f8dd8402655: Starting from their own conception of God, "however limited it was" (<0>p. 47</0>), was enough "to commence spiritual growth" (<1>p. 47</1>). "Afterward, we found ourselves accepting many things which then seemed entirely out of reach." (<2>p. 47</2>).
6db4311b0c0a: Members describe the change as following belief, an attitude <0>and</0> doing: since they came "to believe in a Power greater than themselves, to take a certain attitude toward that Power, and to do certain simple things, there has been a revolutionary change in their way of living and thinking" (<1>p. 50</1>).
5b699fbd6f02: Chapter 7's advice to a newcomer who balks at parts of the program is to tell him "you doubt whether you would have made much progress had you not taken action" (<0>p. 94</0>).
c4939e3ea8ea: Bill's beginning was willingness, then a decision and work: "Upon a foundation of complete willingness I might build what I saw in my friend." (<0>p. 12</0>). At the hospital he offered himself to God, and with his friend made a list of people he had hurt (<1>p. 13</1>).
27955f06ad79: Chapter 11 does show that being there mattered. The Akron weekly meeting was for "anyone or everyone interested in a spiritual way of life" (<0>pp. 159–160</0>), and its prime object was "to provide a time and place where new people might bring their problems" (<1>p. 160</1>). Many a man still dazed from the hospital "has stepped over the threshold of that home into freedom" (<2>p. 160</2>). Already impressed by the members who had visited him, he "capitulated entirely" when he heard a story that matched his own (<3>p. 160</3>).
f283ba5a1915: So the book does picture a newcomer walking in and being changed by what he finds there. But in its telling he comes from the hospital, where members had already visited him and impressed him (<0>p. 160</0>), and the turn is a capitulation, which is a change of mind. Chapter 11 also says plainly that "life among Alcoholics Anonymous is more than attending gatherings and visiting hospitals" (<1>p. 161</1>). See: <2>Is "meeting makers make it" in the Big Book?</2>
c1ee1961db3a: "Twice Gifted" (Part III, fourth edition) is the closest any book here comes to the saying. The writer had been to meetings before, but after she was referred to a liver-transplant clinic and told that if she wanted to live she would have to prove alcohol was no longer part of her life (<0>p. 473</0>), she writes: "I found myself willing, and after some weeks of just showing up, I began to believe that this program could work for me." (<1>p. 474</1>). She then went to meetings every day for six months and worked the Steps with a sponsor (<2>p. 474</2>). In her sentence, willingness comes first and belief follows the weeks of showing up. This is one member's experience, not the program text.
4af43217a71d: The Big Book doesn't say "bring the body." It says bring willingness, an open mind and a desire that comes from within (<0>pp. 46–48</0>, 95, 568), and then act on it; belief and a changed way of thinking come after (<1>pp. 47</1>, 50). Where the saying means "come even if you doubt, and keep acting while belief catches up," the text agrees, provided the doubter is at least willing. Where it means attendance alone does the work, the text doesn't say that. See: <2>Does the Big Book say "fake it till you make it"?</2>

A group answers only to "its own conscience" in its own affairs (<0>p. 563</0>), its leaders "do not govern" (<1>p. 565</1>), it pays its own way and avoids piling up money (<2>p. 564</2>), and its one purpose is carrying the message to the alcoholic who still suffers (<3>p. 563</3>).
70d03e0cff40: <0>Whose decision it is.</0> For its group purpose there is but one ultimate authority, "a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience" (<1>p. 563</1>). c1caa87e12cf: <0>When to look beyond the group.</0> If its plans affect neighbouring groups, they should be consulted; and nobody should take action that might greatly affect A.A. as a whole without conferring with the trustees (<1>p. 563</1>). "On such issues our common welfare is paramount" (<2>p. 563</2>).
a271e26e70d4: <0>The money.</0> The group is supported by its own members' voluntary contributions (<1>p. 564</1>). Large gifts and contributions with strings are unwise, and treasuries that keep growing "beyond prudent reserves" for no stated A.A. purpose are a concern (<2>p. 564</2>).
1ae8e4038252: <0>The officers.</0> A group needs "the least possible organization," rotating leadership is best, and a small group may elect a secretary, a large one a rotating committee (<1>p. 565</1>). They are servants: "They derive no real authority from their titles; they do not govern" (<2>p. 565</2>).

34a7400067b0: Groups instructing delegates. Bill says this right exists, but "good management seldom means the full exercise of a stated set of ultimate rights" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept III). A Conference with all the facts and the debate in front of it will nearly always decide better than delegates bound beforehand. "Nevertheless the ‘instructed’ Delegate who cannot act on his own conscience in a final Conference vote is not a ‘trusted servant’ at all; he is just a messenger" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept III).
67db3d10c1e8: Delegates issuing hasty, flat directives to trustees who know the subject better.
1391101cac68: Trustees managing the service corporations in detail, so that staff "would be turned into buck-passers and rubber stamps; their choice would be to rebel and resign, or to submit and rot" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept III).

Alcoholics "have lost the ability to control our drinking" and "no real alcoholic ever recovers control" (<0>p. 30</0>). Intervals of seeming control were "inevitably followed by still less control" (<1>p. 30</1>). Then the line the saying is usually reaching for: "We are convinced to a man that alcoholics of our type are in the grip of a progressive illness. Over any considerable period we get worse, never better." (<2>p. 30</2>). The image that follows is a man who has lost his legs and never grows new ones (<3>p. 30</3>), and every remedy tried gave at best "brief recovery, followed always by a still worse relapse" (<4>p. 31</4>).
1697376d14d0: Read in its paragraph, "we get worse, never better" is about the drinking career: the attempts to control it, the shrinking intervals, the relapse after each remedy (<0>pp. 30–31</0>). The book doesn't here describe anything happening while a man isn't drinking.
99e10298f374: The nearest it comes is the man of thirty (<0>pp. 32–33</0>). He "remained bone dry for twenty-five years" (<1>p. 32</1>), retired, and believed his long sobriety "had qualified him to drink as other men" (<2>p. 32</2>). In two months he was in hospital; he could not regulate it and then could not stop; "he went to pieces quickly and was dead within four years" (<3>p. 33</3>). The lesson the book draws is exact and worth reading as written: "here is a man who at fifty-five years found he was just where he had left off at thirty" (<4>p. 33</4>). Where he left off: not further along. The book then says "Commencing to drink after a period of sobriety, we are in a short time as bad as ever." (<5>p. 33</5>), and sums it as "Once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic" (<6>p. 33</6>). So the book's claim is that sobriety doesn't earn immunity (<7>p. 33</7>), and that drinking again picks up as bad as before and quickly (<8>p. 33</8>). The push-ups saying adds a step the book doesn't take: that the illness is getting stronger in the meantime. See: <9>Who is the man who stayed sober twenty-five years and drank again ([p. 32](/big-book/page-32/))?</9> and <10>Does the Big Book say "once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic"?</10>
10295dfa079e: Chapter 6 is where the book says what a sober alcoholic is living with. The recovered man finds that "the problem has been removed. It does not exist for us." (<0>p. 85</0>), and in the same breath, "That is how we react so long as we keep in fit spiritual condition." (<1>p. 85</1>). Then: "It is easy to let up on the spiritual program of action and rest on our laurels. We are headed for trouble if we do, for alcohol is a subtle foe. We are not cured of alcoholism." (<2>p. 85</2>). What the member has instead is "a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition" (<3>p. 85</3>).
bcb23e0c5003: This is the thought the saying shares, said the book's way: the condition hasn't gone, and letting up on the program is where the trouble starts (<0>p. 85</0>). The difference is in what is doing the work. The book doesn't picture the illness training; it says the alcoholic is safe "so long as" he keeps at the spiritual program (<1>p. 85</1>), and that the danger is in his own letting up. See: <2>What is the "daily reprieve," and what is it "contingent on"?</2>
